Information since the June meeting remains broadly consistent with the FOMC’s July 26, 2017 statement: labor markets continued to strengthen and economic activity expanded at a modest-to-moderate pace. Beige Book reports across districts (including Atlanta and St. Louis) highlight tight labor markets with shortages of qualified workers for both low- and high-skilled positions, contributing to gradual wage gains. Consumer spending was rising across many districts, and energy activity improved alongside oil and natural gas. Inflation pressures remained subdued, with 12‑month inflation below 2 percent and market-based inflation compensation low, consistent with anchored longer-term expectations.

Credit conditions from the latest SLOOS point to headwinds: weaker loan demand in CRE (construction, land development, and multifamily) and in consumer credit (auto and credit cards), alongside tighter standards in these consumer segments. Demand was roughly unchanged for nonfarm nonresidential loans. Banks eased standards for residential real estate (including jumbo, QM, and GSE mortgages) and kept standards roughly unchanged for home-purchase loans and HELOCs. Foreign banks reported tighter standards for C&I and CRE, with some strength in CRE loan demand. This mix suggests some drag from consumer and CRE credit, partly offset by easier mortgage credit.

Policy implications: With inflation below target, balanced near-term risks, and mixed credit signals, the backdrop supports maintaining an accommodative stance with gradual rate increases and proceeding with balance sheet normalization as previously outlined, while monitoring inflation and credit developments closely.

Net tone: slightly less positive than previously assessed due to the credit headwinds, despite tight labor markets and steady activity.
